rationale: High-yield OP trap: chalazion (chronic granuloma of Meibomian gland) vs hordeolum internum (acute Zeis gland infection) — both are internal but distinct aetiology and management.
Classic OP examination trap: differentiating preseptal from orbital cellulitis — the single most critical distinction in lid disease (Khurana).
MRD-1 measurement is a core clinical skill for ptosis quantification — frequently confused with lid fissure height in finals (Khurana Chapter on Eyelids).
Congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction management — Crigler massage vs probing timing — is a common finals question.
Lid retraction in thyroid eye disease — distinguishing Dalrymple, Kocher and von Graefe signs — is a classic finals spot diagnosis (Khurana, Parsons' 23rd ed).
Sight-threatening thyroid eye disease (DON — dysthyroid optic neuropathy) — urgent orbital decompression indication — core competency.
Chandler's classification of orbital cellulitis — stage determining surgical intervention — is a perennial exam question (Khurana, Parsons').
Optic nerve compromise is the key indication to escalate orbital cellulitis to emergency surgery — discriminating this from routine post-septal disease is essential.
Bilateral involvement as a hallmark of CST vs unilateral orbital cellulitis — a discriminating feature tested in finals (Khurana).
Anticoagulation in CST — controversial but now recommended — and the role of IV antibiotics as first-line management.
Hertel exophthalmometry technique and normal values — practical clinical exam skill from Khurana.
Direction of proptosis as a localising sign — a key examination tool for narrowing the differential of orbital masses (Khurana, Parsons').
Cavernous haemangioma — the commonest benign intraconal adult orbital tumour — and its imaging signature are classic viva and MCQ material (Khurana, Parsons').
Red flag signs for malignant orbital tumour requiring urgent referral — distinguishing from benign lesions is a core MBBS competency.
